REPETITIVE MOTION INJURY (ERGONOMICS) STANDARD — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Acme Corp

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
Acme Corp maintains this Repetitive Motion Injury (Ergonomics) Standard information sheet to describe what California's Cal/OSHA ergonomics regulation, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5110, says about workplace repetitive motion injuries. The regulation applies only after a specific trigger has been met — more than one employee has incurred a physician-diagnosed, work-related repetitive motion injury while performing identical work activity, reported to the employer within a 12-month window — and then requires the employer to establish a program consisting of a worksite evaluation, control of the exposures that caused the injuries, and employee training. This document describes the statute that directed the Occupational Safety and Health Standards Board to adopt an ergonomics standard (Labor Code section 6357), each element of the regulation as it now reads, the regulation's own "satisfaction of an employer's obligation" provision, and the Court of Appeal decision that reviewed the standard shortly after its adoption. It states information about the regulation as it relates to employees such as Jordan Alex Lee; it does not determine whether the regulation has been triggered at any particular worksite or whether any particular employer has complied with it.

Employer: Acme Corp
Employee: Jordan Alex Lee
Program contact: Taylor Morgan

STATUTORY MANDATE FOR AN ERGONOMICS STANDARD (LABOR CODE § 6357)
The regulation traces to a 1993 statute. Labor Code section 6357 provides that "[o]n or before January 1, 1995, the Occupational Safety and Health Standards Board shall adopt standards for ergonomics in the workplace designed to minimize the instances of injury from repetitive motion." The section was added by Statutes 1993, chapter 121, section 71, effective July 16, 1993. The Standards Board adopted 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5110 in response; the regulation's authority note cites Labor Code sections 142.3 and 6357, and its history note records that the section was filed June 3, 1997 and became operative July 3, 1997 — more than two years after the statutory deadline.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "On or before January 1, 1995, the Occupational Safety and Health Standards Board shall adopt standards for ergonomics in the workplace designed to minimize the instances of injury from repetitive motion."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 6357 (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Labor Code § 6357 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=6357.)
  "(Added by Stats. 1993, Ch. 121, Sec. 71. Effective July 16, 1993.)"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 6357 (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Labor Code § 6357 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=6357.)
  "Note: Authority cited: Sections 142.3 and 6357, Labor Code. Reference: Sections 142.3 and 6357, Labor Code; and Pulaski v. Occupational Safety & Health Stds. Bd. (1999) 75 Cal.App.4th 1315 [90 Cal. Rptr. 2d 54]."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5110 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 5110 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5110.html)
  "1. New article 106 (section 5110) and section filed 6-3-97; operative 7-3-97 (Register 97, No. 23)."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5110 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 5110 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5110.html)
  Known gap: Labor Code section 6357 is a one-sentence directive to the Standards Board; it does not itself impose duties on employers. The adoption and operative dates are taken from the regulation's history note on the Department of Industrial Relations Title 8 page and were not separately verified against the California Regulatory Notice Register. Labor Code section 142.3 (the Board's general standard-setting authority, also cited in the regulation's authority note) was not independently fetched for this document.

SCOPE: THE STANDARD APPLIES ONLY AFTER MULTIPLE REPETITIVE MOTION INJURIES
The regulation does not apply to every job that involves repetitive motion. Under 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5110(a), the section "shall apply to a job, process, or operation where a repetitive motion injury (RMI) has occurred to more than one employee under the following conditions," and it then lists four conditions — work-related causation, a relationship between the injuries at the workplace, medical requirements, and time requirements — all of which must be present. The first condition, "[w]ork related causation," is met where "[t]he repetitive motion injuries (RMIs) were predominantly caused (i.e. 50% or more) by a repetitive job, process, or operation." The second condition, "[r]elationship between RMIs at the workplace," requires that "[t]he employees incurring the RMIs were performing a job, process, or operation of identical work activity," and the regulation defines that phrase: "Identical work activity means that the employees were performing the same repetitive motion task, such as but not limited to word processing, assembly, or loading."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "This section shall apply to a job, process, or operation where a repetitive motion injury (RMI) has occurred to more than one employee under the following conditions:"
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5110 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 5110, subd. (a) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5110.html)
  "Work related causation. The repetitive motion injuries (RMIs) were predominantly caused (i.e. 50% or more) by a repetitive job, process, or operation;"
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5110 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 5110, subd. (a)(1) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5110.html)
  "Relationship between RMIs at the workplace. The employees incurring the RMIs were performing a job, process, or operation of identical work activity. Identical work activity means that the employees were performing the same repetitive motion task, such as but not limited to word processing, assembly, or loading;"
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5110 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 5110, subd. (a)(2) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5110.html)
  Known gap: The regulation does not define "repetitive motion injury" beyond the musculoskeletal-injury and physician-diagnosis requirements in subdivision (a)(3), and it does not specify how the 50 percent causation determination is to be made or by whom. Whether a given set of injuries meets the "identical work activity" test is a fact question the regulation's text does not resolve.

MEDICAL DIAGNOSIS AND 12-MONTH REPORTING REQUIREMENTS
The third and fourth conditions in 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5110(a) concern medical confirmation and timing. The medical requirement is that "[t]he RMIs were musculoskeletal injuries that a licensed physician objectively identified and diagnosed." The time requirement is that "[t]he RMIs were reported by the employees to the employer in the last 12 months but not before July 3, 1997." Because the injuries must have been reported to the employer, the trigger is tied to employee reports rather than to the date an injury occurred or was diagnosed, and the 12-month window is measured backward from the present. The July 3, 1997 floor corresponds to the regulation's operative date recorded in its history note, so injuries reported before the standard took effect do not count toward the trigger.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "Medical requirements. The RMIs were musculoskeletal injuries that a licensed physician objectively identified and diagnosed; and"
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5110 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 5110, subd. (a)(3) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5110.html)
  "Time requirements. The RMIs were reported by the employees to the employer in the last 12 months but not before July 3, 1997."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5110 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 5110, subd. (a)(4) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5110.html)
  "1. New article 106 (section 5110) and section filed 6-3-97; operative 7-3-97 (Register 97, No. 23)."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5110 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 5110 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5110.html)
  Known gap: The regulation does not specify the form a report to the employer must take, does not address injuries diagnosed by licensed health care providers other than physicians, and does not state how the 12-month window operates where two qualifying injuries were reported more than 12 months apart. The explanation that the July 3, 1997 date corresponds to the operative date is drawn from the regulation's history note rather than from the text of subdivision (a)(4) itself.

REQUIRED PROGRAM TO MINIMIZE REPETITIVE MOTION INJURIES
Once the trigger in subdivision (a) is met, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5110(b) imposes an affirmative duty: "Every employer subject to this section shall establish and implement a program designed to minimize RMIs." The regulation prescribes the program's three components: "The program shall include a worksite evaluation, control of exposures which have caused RMIs and training of employees." Each component is then elaborated in subdivisions (b)(1) through (b)(3). The text of the regulation does not require the program to be in writing, does not set a deadline for establishing it, and does not require it to be submitted to or approved by the Division of Occupational Safety and Health.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "Program designated to minimize RMIs. Every employer subject to this section shall establish and implement a program designed to minimize RMIs. The program shall include a worksite evaluation, control of exposures which have caused RMIs and training of employees."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5110 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 5110, subd. (b) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5110.html)
  Known gap: The regulation is silent on whether the ergonomics program must be a separate document or may be incorporated into the employer's Injury and Illness Prevention Program under 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203, which was not fetched for this document. The statements that the regulation does not require a writing, a deadline, or agency approval are observations about what the text does not contain, not a description of any enforcement position of the Division.

PROGRAM ELEMENT ONE: WORKSITE EVALUATION
The first required program element under 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5110(b)(1) is a worksite evaluation: "Each job, process, or operation of identical work activity covered by this section or a representative number of such jobs, processes, or operations of identical work activities shall be evaluated for exposures which have caused RMIs." The evaluation is directed at the covered jobs, processes, or operations — those where the qualifying injuries occurred — and the regulation allows the employer to evaluate a representative number rather than every instance of the identical work activity. The evaluation's stated object is the "exposures which have caused RMIs," not workplace ergonomic hazards generally.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "Worksite evaluation. Each job, process, or operation of identical work activity covered by this section or a representative number of such jobs, processes, or operations of identical work activities shall be evaluated for exposures which have caused RMIs."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5110 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 5110, subd. (b)(1) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5110.html)
  "2. Editorial correction of subsection (b)(1) (Register 97, No. 29)."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5110 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 5110 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5110.html)
  Known gap: The regulation does not define what constitutes a "representative number" of jobs, does not specify who must conduct the evaluation or what qualifications they must have, and does not prescribe any particular evaluation method or documentation. The history note records an editorial correction of subsection (b)(1) in 1997 (Register 97, No. 29); the pre-correction wording was not examined.

PROGRAM ELEMENT TWO: CONTROL OF EXPOSURES THAT CAUSED INJURIES
The second required program element, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5110(b)(2), addresses correction: "Any exposures that caused RMIs shall, in a timely manner, be corrected or if not capable of being corrected have the exposures minimized to the extent feasible." The regulation identifies two categories of controls the employer must consider, with examples of each: "The employer shall consider engineering controls, such as work station redesign, adjustable fixtures or tool redesign, and administrative controls, such as job rotation, work pacing or work breaks." The text thus establishes a correct-if-possible, otherwise-minimize-to-the-extent-feasible standard and requires consideration of both engineering and administrative approaches, without mandating any particular control for any particular exposure.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "Control of exposures which have caused RMIs. Any exposures that caused RMIs shall, in a timely manner, be corrected or if not capable of being corrected have the exposures minimized to the extent feasible. The employer shall consider engineering controls, such as work station redesign, adjustable fixtures or tool redesign, and administrative controls, such as job rotation, work pacing or work breaks."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5110 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 5110, subd. (b)(2) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5110.html)
  Known gap: The regulation does not define "in a timely manner" or "to the extent feasible," and it does not rank engineering controls above administrative controls (unlike some other Cal/OSHA standards that prescribe a hierarchy of controls). The listed controls are illustrative examples introduced by "such as," not an exhaustive or mandatory list.

PROGRAM ELEMENT THREE: EMPLOYEE TRAINING
The third required program element, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5110(b)(3), is training. "Employees shall be provided training that includes an explanation of" five subjects: "(A) The employer's program; (B) The exposures which have been associated with RMIs; (C) The symptoms and consequences of injuries caused by repetitive motion; (D) The importance of reporting symptoms and injuries to the employer; and (E) Methods used by the employer to minimize RMIs." The training requirement is phrased in terms of content that must be explained; the regulation does not specify the frequency, format, duration, or language of the training, does not limit training to employees performing the affected work activity, and does not require that training be documented.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]

  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5110 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 5110, subd. (b)(3) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5110.html)
  "The employer's program;"
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5110 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 5110, subd. (b)(3)(A) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5110.html)
  "The exposures which have been associated with RMIs;"
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5110 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 5110, subd. (b)(3)(B) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5110.html)
  "The symptoms and consequences of injuries caused by repetitive motion;"
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5110 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 5110, subd. (b)(3)(C) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5110.html)
  "The importance of reporting symptoms and injuries to the employer; and"
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5110 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 5110, subd. (b)(3)(D) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5110.html)
  "Methods used by the employer to minimize RMIs."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5110 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 5110, subd. (b)(3)(E) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5110.html)
  Known gap: The five-subject list is quoted from the Department of Industrial Relations Title 8 page with the lettered items joined into a single sentence for readability; in the source each lettered item appears on its own line, and the citations below quote each item separately. The observations about what the training provision does not specify are drawn from the absence of such terms in the regulation's text; separate Cal/OSHA training and documentation duties under the Injury and Illness Prevention Program standard (8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203) were not examined for this document.

WHEN AN EMPLOYER'S MEASURES SATISFY THE STANDARD
8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5110(c), titled "Satisfaction of an employer's obligation," limits how an employer's chosen measures may be second-guessed. It provides: "Measures implemented by an employer under subsection (b)(1), (b)(2), or (b)(3) shall satisfy the employer's obligation under that respective subsection, unless it is shown that a measure known to but not taken by the employer is substantially certain to cause a greater reduction in such injuries and that this alternative measure would not impose additional unreasonable costs." Under this text, measures actually implemented for each program element are deemed sufficient unless three things are shown together: an alternative measure was known to the employer, that alternative is substantially certain to produce a greater reduction in injuries, and it would not impose additional unreasonable costs.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "Satisfaction of an employer's obligation. Measures implemented by an employer under subsection (b)(1), (b)(2), or (b)(3) shall satisfy the employer's obligation under that respective subsection, unless it is shown that a measure known to but not taken by the employer is substantially certain to cause a greater reduction in such injuries and that this alternative measure would not impose additional unreasonable costs."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5110 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 5110, subd. (c) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5110.html)
  Known gap: The regulation does not say who bears the burden of making the showing described in subdivision (c) or in what proceeding it would be made, and it does not define "substantially certain" or "unreasonable costs." This clause describes the text only; how the Occupational Safety and Health Appeals Board has applied subdivision (c) in citation appeals was not researched for this document.

JUDICIAL REVIEW OF THE STANDARD: PULASKI V. CALIFORNIA OCCUPATIONAL SAFETY & HEALTH STANDARDS BOARD (1999)
The regulation's authority note cites Pulaski v. California Occupational Safety & Health Standards Board (1999) 75 Cal.App.4th 1315, in which the Third District Court of Appeal reviewed the standard shortly after its adoption. The court described the standard's origin in Labor Code section 6357: "In response to this legislative mandate, and following a protracted saga of rulemaking, comments and public hearings, Cal OSHA's Standards Board (the Board) promulgated title 8, section 5110 of the California Code of Regulations (Regulation 5110)." It noted that "[n]o sooner was the ink dry on the final regulation than it came under attack from opposite directions" — labor interests contending the regulation was too weak and business interests contending it was unauthorized. The trial court had "struck four portions of Regulation 5110, found the remainder of the regulation valid, and ordered it to go into effect as modified by the court." On appeal, the Court of Appeal stated it would "conclude that, except for one conspicuous exemption, the regulation is valid, that the trial court improperly invaded the rulemaking authority of the Board by striking the remaining provisions, and that the APA-based challenges to the regulation are meritless." The exemption at issue was the regulation's original small-employer exemption, under which "[e]mployers with nine or fewer employees are completely exempted from the regulation (the 'small employer exemption')." The trial court had "ruled this provision was inconsistent with the Board's statutory mandate to minimize RMI's in the workplace," and the Court of Appeal stated: "On this count we agree with the trial court." It characterized the defect as structural rather than discretionary — "the exemption constitutes an unauthorized diminishment of the Board's regulatory authority and is invalid per se" — and held the exemption severable: "Regulation 5110 is a valid, self-contained regulation, save for one exemption which contradicts the statutory mandate. Severing the invalid exemption would not change or alter the substance of the standard; rather its only effect would be to increase the scope of its coverage." The court also referred to subdivision (c) as "the 'safe harbor' provision." The disposition was: "The judgment is reversed. The cause is remanded to the trial court to enter a new judgment granting and denying the petitions in accordance with the views expressed here." Consistent with that decision, the regulation's history note records a 2000 change without regulatory effect "repealing subsection (a)(4) Exemption," which is why the regulation as it now reads contains no small-employer exemption and applies to employers of any size once its trigger is met.

  Known gap: Fetch-path disclosure: the CourtListener API daily quota shared across parallel agents was exhausted for the entire period this document was prepared, and the CourtListener web page for the opinion returned an HTTP 202 bot-challenge response to curl, while Justia, FindLaw, Google Scholar, case.law, Leagle, and the Wayback Machine were all egress-blocked. The Pulaski quotations in this clause were therefore reconstructed from CourtListener's public Atom search feed (https://www.courtlistener.com/feed/search/) by issuing exact-phrase queries scoped to the opinion's cluster id (2300696) and merging the overlapping highlighted snippets the feed returned; every quotation was then re-verified by submitting the full quotation as a single exact-phrase query against the same feed and confirming the Pulaski entry was returned. That verification is token-level (the search engine ignores punctuation and quotation-mark style), so minor punctuation or quotation-mark differences from the opinion as printed in the official reporter are possible; the opinion's single quotation marks around 'small employer exemption' and 'safe harbor' are rendered here as nested quotes. The full opinion was not read end to end, so this clause does not describe the court's reasoning on the other three provisions the trial court had struck (including the work-related-causation and physician-diagnosis conditions) beyond the court's summary statement that striking them improperly invaded the Board's rulemaking authority. expectedJSON.gap: The regulation does not define "repetitive motion injury" beyond the musculoskeletal-injury and physician-diagnosis requirements in subdivision (a)(3), and it does not specify how the 50 percent causation determination is to be made or by whom. Whether a given set of injuries meets the "identical work activity" test is a fact question the regulation's text does not resolve.

expectedJSON.body: The third and fourth conditions in 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5110(a) concern medical confirmation and timing. The medical requirement is that "[t]he RMIs were musculoskeletal injuries that a licensed physician objectively identified and diagnosed." The time requirement is that "[t]he RMIs were reported by the employees to the employer in the last 12 months but not before July 3, 1997." Because the injuries must have been reported to the employer, the trigger is tied to employee reports rather than to the date an injury occurred or was diagnosed, and the 12-month window is measured backward from the present. The July 3, 1997 floor corresponds to the regulation's operative date recorded in its history note, so injuries reported before the standard took effect do not count toward the trigger.

expectedJSON.gap: The regulation does not specify the form a report to the employer must take, does not address injuries diagnosed by licensed health care providers other than physicians, and does not state how the 12-month window operates where two qualifying injuries were reported more than 12 months apart. The explanation that the July 3, 1997 date corresponds to the operative date is drawn from the regulation's history note rather than from the text of subdivision (a)(4) itself.

expectedJSON.body: Once the trigger in subdivision (a) is met, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5110(b) imposes an affirmative duty: "Every employer subject to this section shall establish and implement a program designed to minimize RMIs." The regulation prescribes the program's three components: "The program shall include a worksite evaluation, control of exposures which have caused RMIs and training of employees." Each component is then elaborated in subdivisions (b)(1) through (b)(3). The text of the regulation does not require the program to be in writing, does not set a deadline for establishing it, and does not require it to be submitted to or approved by the Division of Occupational Safety and Health.

expectedJSON.gap: The regulation is silent on whether the ergonomics program must be a separate document or may be incorporated into the employer's Injury and Illness Prevention Program under 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203, which was not fetched for this document. The statements that the regulation does not require a writing, a deadline, or agency approval are observations about what the text does not contain, not a description of any enforcement position of the Division.

expectedJSON.body: The first required program element under 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5110(b)(1) is a worksite evaluation: "Each job, process, or operation of identical work activity covered by this section or a representative number of such jobs, processes, or operations of identical work activities shall be evaluated for exposures which have caused RMIs." The evaluation is directed at the covered jobs, processes, or operations — those where the qualifying injuries occurred — and the regulation allows the employer to evaluate a representative number rather than every instance of the identical work activity. The evaluation's stated object is the "exposures which have caused RMIs," not workplace ergonomic hazards generally.

expectedJSON.gap: The regulation does not define what constitutes a "representative number" of jobs, does not specify who must conduct the evaluation or what qualifications they must have, and does not prescribe any particular evaluation method or documentation. The history note records an editorial correction of subsection (b)(1) in 1997 (Register 97, No. 29); the pre-correction wording was not examined.

expectedJSON.body: The second required program element, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5110(b)(2), addresses correction: "Any exposures that caused RMIs shall, in a timely manner, be corrected or if not capable of being corrected have the exposures minimized to the extent feasible." The regulation identifies two categories of controls the employer must consider, with examples of each: "The employer shall consider engineering controls, such as work station redesign, adjustable fixtures or tool redesign, and administrative controls, such as job rotation, work pacing or work breaks." The text thus establishes a correct-if-possible, otherwise-minimize-to-the-extent-feasible standard and requires consideration of both engineering and administrative approaches, without mandating any particular control for any particular exposure.

The employer shall consider engineering controls, such as work station redesign, adjustable fixtures or tool redesign, and administrative controls, such as job rotation, work pacing or work breaks.

expectedJSON.gap: The regulation does not define "in a timely manner" or "to the extent feasible," and it does not rank engineering controls above administrative controls (unlike some other Cal/OSHA standards that prescribe a hierarchy of controls). The listed controls are illustrative examples introduced by "such as," not an exhaustive or mandatory list.

expectedJSON.body: The third required program element, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5110(b)(3), is training. "Employees shall be provided training that includes an explanation of" five subjects: "(A) The employer's program; (B) The exposures which have been associated with RMIs; (C) The symptoms and consequences of injuries caused by repetitive motion; (D) The importance of reporting symptoms and injuries to the employer; and (E) Methods used by the employer to minimize RMIs." The training requirement is phrased in terms of content that must be explained; the regulation does not specify the frequency, format, duration, or language of the training, does not limit training to employees performing the affected work activity, and does not require that training be documented.

expectedJSON.body: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5110(c), titled "Satisfaction of an employer's obligation," limits how an employer's chosen measures may be second-guessed. It provides: "Measures implemented by an employer under subsection (b)(1), (b)(2), or (b)(3) shall satisfy the employer's obligation under that respective subsection, unless it is shown that a measure known to but not taken by the employer is substantially certain to cause a greater reduction in such injuries and that this alternative measure would not impose additional unreasonable costs." Under this text, measures actually implemented for each program element are deemed sufficient unless three things are shown together: an alternative measure was known to the employer, that alternative is substantially certain to produce a greater reduction in injuries, and it would not impose additional unreasonable costs.

This clause describes the text only; how the Occupational Safety and Health Appeals Board has applied subdivision (c) in citation appeals was not researched for this document.

expectedJSON.body: The regulation's authority note cites Pulaski v. California Occupational Safety & Health Standards Board (1999) 75 Cal.App.4th 1315, in which the Third District Court of Appeal reviewed the standard shortly after its adoption. The court described the standard's origin in Labor Code section 6357: "In response to this legislative mandate, and following a protracted saga of rulemaking, comments and public hearings, Cal OSHA's Standards Board (the Board) promulgated title 8, section 5110 of the California Code of Regulations (Regulation 5110)." It noted that "[n]o sooner was the ink dry on the final regulation than it came under attack from opposite directions" — labor interests contending the regulation was too weak and business interests contending it was unauthorized. The trial court had "struck four portions of Regulation 5110, found the remainder of the regulation valid, and ordered it to go into effect as modified by the court." On appeal, the Court of Appeal stated it would "conclude that, except for one conspicuous exemption, the regulation is valid, that the trial court improperly invaded the rulemaking authority of the Board by striking the remaining provisions, and that the APA-based challenges to the regulation are meritless." The exemption at issue was the regulation's original small-employer exemption, under which "[e]mployers with nine or fewer employees are completely exempted from the regulation (the 'small employer exemption')." The trial court had "ruled this provision was inconsistent with the Board's statutory mandate to minimize RMI's in the workplace," and the Court of Appeal stated: "On this count we agree with the trial court." It characterized the defect as structural rather than discretionary — "the exemption constitutes an unauthorized diminishment of the Board's regulatory authority and is invalid per se" — and held the exemption severable: "Regulation 5110 is a valid, self-contained regulation, save for one exemption which contradicts the statutory mandate. Severing the invalid exemption would not change or alter the substance of the standard; rather its only effect would be to increase the scope of its coverage." The court also referred to subdivision (c) as "the 'safe harbor' provision." The disposition was: "The judgment is reversed. The cause is remanded to the trial court to enter a new judgment granting and denying the petitions in accordance with the views expressed here." Consistent with that decision, the regulation's history note records a 2000 change without regulatory effect "repealing subsection (a)(4) Exemption," which is why the regulation as it now reads contains no small-employer exemption and applies to employers of any size once its trigger is met.

expectedJSON.gap: Fetch-path disclosure: the CourtListener API daily quota shared across parallel agents was exhausted for the entire period this document was prepared, and the CourtListener web page for the opinion returned an HTTP 202 bot-challenge response to curl, while Justia, FindLaw, Google Scholar, case.law, Leagle, and the Wayback Machine were all egress-blocked. The Pulaski quotations in this clause were therefore reconstructed from CourtListener's public Atom search feed (https://www.courtlistener.com/feed/search/) by issuing exact-phrase queries scoped to the opinion's cluster id (2300696) and merging the overlapping highlighted snippets the feed returned; every quotation was then re-verified by submitting the full quotation as a single exact-phrase query against the same feed and confirming the Pulaski entry was returned. That verification is token-level (the search engine ignores punctuation and quotation-mark style), so minor punctuation or quotation-mark differences from the opinion as printed in the official reporter are possible; the opinion's single quotation marks around 'small employer exemption' and 'safe harbor' are rendered here as nested quotes. The full opinion was not read end to end, so this clause does not describe the court's reasoning on the other three provisions the trial court had struck (including the work-related-causation and physician-diagnosis conditions) beyond the court's summary statement that striking them improperly invaded the Board's rulemaking authority. The characterization of the two sides' positions as 'too weak' and 'unauthorized' is a paraphrase of the court's description of the labor and business challenges, not a quotation.
